content: Folic acid is an orally administered nutritive agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of megaloblastic anemia caused by folic acid deficiency. It is also used in anemias of nutritional origin, pregnancy, infancy, or childhood. Common side effects include erythema, skin rash, itching, general malaise, and respiratory difficulty. For adults, the usual therapeutic dose is up to 1 mg daily, regardless of age. Higher doses may be required in resistant cases. Once clinical symptoms resolve and blood parameters normalize, maintenance doses are recommended: 0.1 mg for infants, up to 0.3 mg for children under 4 years, 0.4 mg for adults and children aged 4 years or older, and 0.8 mg for pregnant and lactating women. Doses exceeding 0.1 mg daily should not be used unless vitamin B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being treated, as folic acid can mask the hematologic symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency while allowing neurological damage to progress. In cases of alcoholism, hemolytic anemia, anticonvulsant therapy, or chronic infection, maintenance doses may need to be increased. Folic acid is contraindicated in patients with known intolerance to the drug. It is not appropriate as sole therapy for pernicious anemia or other megaloblastic anemias caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. High doses of folic acid can obscure the diagnosis of pernicious anemia by improving hematologic symptoms while allowing neurological complications to worsen. Adequate vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary to prevent or treat these neurological effects. Adverse reactions to folic acid are rare but may include allergic sensitization, such as erythema, rash, itching, malaise, and respiratory difficulty due to bronchospasm. Gastrointestinal side effects, such as anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension, flatulence, and a bitter taste, have been reported with high doses (e.g., 15 mg daily). Neurological effects, including altered sleep patterns, irritability, overactivity, mental depression, and impaired judgment, have also been observed. Prolonged use may decrease serum vitamin B12 levels. Folic acid has been reported to increase seizure frequency in some epileptic patients taking anticonvulsants like phenobarbital, primidone, or phenytoin. Folic acid interacts with certain drugs. It may antagonize the anticonvulsant effects of phenytoin, requiring dose adjustments to maintain seizure control. Folate deficiency can result from increased loss (e.g., during renal dialysis) or interference with metabolism (e.g., by methotrexate or alcohol). Antibiotics like tetracycline may suppress Lactobacillus casei, leading to falsely low serum and red cell folate levels. During pregnancy, folic acid is classified as Category A by the FDA, indicating no evidence of fetal harm. Folic acid requirements increase significantly during pregnancy, and deficiency can result in fetal damage. It is excreted in breast milk, and supplementation may be necessary for low-birth-weight infants or those with infections or prolonged diarrhea. Folic acid is rapidly absorbed in the proximal small intestine and appears in plasma within 15–30 minutes after oral administration. Peak levels are reached within an hour. It is metabolized in the liver to tetrahydrofolic acid, which is essential for nucleic acid synthesis and erythropoiesis. Excess folic acid is excreted in urine, with most of the dose eliminated within 24 hours. Folic acid tablets (1 mg) are yellow, round, and scored, containing inactive ingredients such as lactose monohydrate, microcrystalline cellulose, sodium starch glycolate, and stearic acid. They should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F) in a well-closed, child-resistant container.
